sections.8.0:
Chapter 7 covered the base Bitcoin blockchain — secure, but slow and relatively costly for small everyday purchases like a taxi fare or a loaf of bread. This chapter covers the Lightning Network, a layer built on top of Bitcoin specifically to make small, fast, cheap payments practical.

Activity: watch "Bitcoin Lightning Network Explained: How it Actually Works" before continuing — seeing it visualized helps before we get into the mechanics.
sections.8.1:
The Lightning Network works by opening payment channels between participants, backed by real bitcoin locked on the base blockchain. Once a channel is open, participants can send any number of near-instant, near-free payments back and forth, with only the opening and closing of the channel actually touching the base blockchain.

In practice, most users don't manage channels directly — wallet apps and payment processors (like the ones behind EkasiPay) handle this in the background, so using Lightning feels as simple as scanning a QR code.
sections.8.2: Just like on-chain wallets in Chapter 7, Lightning wallets come in different flavors depending on who holds the keys and channels.
sections.8.2.1: A self-custodial Lightning wallet means you manage your own channels and keys directly — full control, but more technical responsibility. A custodial Lightning wallet means a service manages channels on your behalf — much simpler for a merchant or new user, at the cost of trusting that provider, same tradeoff as Chapter 7's custodial/self-custodial distinction.
sections.8.2.2: The same open-source vs closed-source distinction from Chapter 7 applies here too — open-source Lightning wallets let the community verify the code actually does what it claims.
sections.8.3: Setting up a Lightning wallet typically takes minutes on a custodial option — download an app, and you're ready to send and receive. Self-custodial Lightning setups involve more steps (managing channel liquidity, backups), which is why many people start custodial for everyday spending and move to self-custody as their balances and confidence grow.
sections.8.4:
Sending a Lightning payment usually means scanning a QR code (called an 'invoice') generated by the receiver, confirming the amount, and sending — the payment typically settles in under a second.

Activity: do the Lightning Wallet Relay Race with your group — pass a small payment quickly from person to person and feel just how different the speed is from an on-chain transaction.
sections.8.5: This is where Bitcoin stops being theoretical and becomes something you use at the till. Lightning's speed and low fees make it genuinely practical for daily spending in a way base-layer Bitcoin generally isn't.
sections.8.5.1: Online, many e-commerce platforms support Lightning through payment plugins — a shopper scans a QR code at checkout instead of entering card details, and the merchant receives payment almost instantly with no chargeback risk.
sections.8.5.2: In person, look for the Lightning-accepting merchants already active in our own community — Bitcoin Ekasi's EkasiPay network now covers 65 merchants across Mossel Bay who accept Lightning payments directly. This isn't a hypothetical example from somewhere else; it's happening at shops you can walk to.
sections.8.5.3: For merchants and customers still getting comfortable with Lightning directly, gift cards and prepaid payment cards that convert to and from bitcoin act as a bridge — familiar to use, while still connecting to Bitcoin underneath.
sections.8.5.4:
A circular economy is one where bitcoin earned locally gets spent locally too — at merchants, on transport, between neighbors — rather than immediately converting back to rand. Every new merchant who accepts Lightning strengthens that circle, and every person who spends bitcoin locally instead of cashing straight out reinforces it further.

This is exactly what the EkasiPay network you may already be familiar with is built to grow — Bitcoin as something genuinely usable in daily life here, not just an investment held somewhere abstract.
